edits.find:
⚠︎ Two ledgers on the early-screening trigger Exam ledger (bank, verbatim): DEXA "at age 65 years or earlier in those who have at least one risk factor — family history of hip fracture, prior fragility fracture, smoking history, low BMI, or use of corticosteroids."
Clinic ledger (USPSTF): under 65, screen when FRAX 10-year major osteoporotic risk ≥9.3%. The bank's version is the operational shorthand; the exam scores the shorthand.
edits.with:
⚠︎ Exam answer versus clinical practice Exam answer: DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) at age 65 years, or earlier in those who have at least one risk factor. The listed risk factors are family history of hip fracture, prior fragility fracture, smoking history, low BMI (body mass index) and use of corticosteroids.
Clinical practice: the USPSTF (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force) uses the FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) under 65. It screens when the FRAX 10-year major osteoporotic risk ≥9.3%. The risk-factor list is the operational shorthand, and the exam scores it.

A parent's hip fracture counts on the exam and in FRAX; a sibling's counts on the exam but not in FRAX.

edits.find: Morbidity ≠ death. Morbidity is disease burden — complications, disability. Mortality is death. They're paired precisely because they differ. "Prevent disease-related morbidity" in a diabetic means prevent the complications of diabetes, and the annual dilated eye exam catches the most common preventable one: retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced and the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults.

edits.find:
Short stature is a height at or below the 2nd percentile, but the decider is velocity, not height. A child who tracks a low but steady channel has a normal variant (familial short stature or constitutional delay); a child who crosses 2 or more major percentile lines (for example 25th to 10th to 2nd) has pathologic growth failure. Then read weight against height: weight falls first in malnutrition and gut disease such as celiac disease or IBD; height falls first with weight preserved or rising in endocrine disease (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, glucocorticoid excess). Bone age is the first test: delayed bone age means growth potential remains; advanced bone age means sex steroid exposure.

The evaluation runs in a fixed order. Dysmorphic features come first and send you to a genetic cause (Turner syndrome, Down syndrome, skeletal dysplasia) and a karyotype. Without them, velocity splits the rest. Impaired velocity with a delayed bone age is endocrine disease, malnutrition or systemic illness (IBD, celiac, kidney disease); an advanced bone age is precocious puberty, a child tall now who ends up short. Normal velocity with delayed puberty and bone age is constitutional delay; normal velocity with normal puberty and bone age is familial or idiopathic short stature.

This girl has falling height velocity, preserved weight, delayed bone age, fatigue and bradycardia: acquired hypothyroidism. Her puberty shows the thelarche and adrenarche split: hypothyroidism suppresses gonadotropins, so breasts stay Tanner 1, while adrenal androgens still drive pubic hair to Tanner 4. Constitutional delay shares the delayed bone age and late puberty but keeps a normal velocity and causes no symptoms.
